newsitem.title: USA: Buffett sees Berkshire book value gains slowing.
newsitem.headline: Buffett sees Berkshire book value gains slowing.

text.p: Berkshire Hathaway Inc has posted gains in per share book value of 23.8 percent compounded annually for the past 32 years, but chairman Warren Buffett cautioned that, going forward, that index is unlikely to show growth of more than 15 percent a year.
"I think 15 percent is absolutely tops," Buffett said at the company's annual shareholders' meeting here. "It could be very substantially lower than that."
At the end of 1996, the company's per share book value stood at $19,011.
As the billionaire investment guru's company has grown, he said, it has had to find places to invest ever larger amounts of money.

"The larger amount of capital we have to work with, the harder the job is," he said. "We've had a terrific market that has reappraised all businesses in the last 15 years. We've been aided by a tailwind, but we won't have that tailwind in the future, I can assure you of that. And the larger amount of capital is an anchor," he told shareholders.

Buffett, named the world's second richest man by Forbes magazine last year, answered questions from shareholders for several hours after formally adjourning the business part of the meeting less than 10 minutes after it began.

One shareholder asked Buffett about a comment he made in his latest annual letter to shareholders, in which he expressed the opinion that most stocks might currently be overvalued. Had he made this comment, the shareholder asked, in league with Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan's warning about the "irrational exuberance" of the stock market?
"No," Buffett answered. "It's very hard to understand what Alan says sometimes, so it's not much use talking to him.
"My comment was not a market prediction in any sense," Buffett adeded. "We never try to predict the market."
He added that Berkshire had no intention to sell its major holdings, which include large stakes in Coca-Cola Co and McDonald's Corp.
Berkshire Hathaway's share price has long been one of the loftiest on Wall Street. It traded Monday at $39,000, up $1000.
Last year for the first time the company issued B shares, valued at 1/30th of the A shares. But Buffett said he planned no further steps to reduce the share price.
The Class B shares were trading up $35 to $1305.
"We will not be splitting Berkshire's stock," he said. "We do not consider that a pro-shareholder move. If we did, we'd do it".

With the steep price of the A shares, Buffett said, "I think we have a more investment-oriented audience in this room today than we might otherwise have. It's a way of enticing certain types of investors and discouraging others."
